pages.name: Where outputs land
pages.text: Every output is a mix of the matrix’s columns. The input’s numbers say how much of each. Take `A = [1 2; 2 4]`. An input `(x, y)` gives x lots of `(1, 2)` and y lots of `(2, 4)`. But y lots of `(2, 4)` is 2y lots of `(1, 2)`. So every output is `(x + 2y)` lots of `(1, 2)`. Everything A reaches, its [[column space]], is the line through `(1, 2)`. Zero lots of each column give zero, so it always holds the origin.

pages.name: Which can it reach?
pages.why: Every output is some lots of `(1, 2)`. `(−1, −2)` is −1 lot of `(1, 2)`, so the input `(−1, 0)` reaches it. `(2, 1)` and `(1, 3)` are not lots of `(1, 2)`, so no input reaches them.

pages.name: What it crushes
pages.text: Now find what it crushes. The input `(2, −1)` gives 2 lots of `(1, 2)` and −1 lot of `(2, 4)`. That is the zero arrow. Everything A crushes to zero is its [[null space]], here the line through `(2, −1)`. A step of `(2, −1)` leaves `x + 2y` the same, as `2 + 2 × (−1) = 0`. So the output does not move. Both `(1, 1)` and `(3, 0)` land on `(3, 6)`.

pages.name: Another input
pages.task: The input `(1, 1)` lands on `(3, 6)`. Which other input lands there too?
pages.why: An answer plus a step along the null space is still an answer. `(1, 1) + (2, −1) = (3, 0)`. Check it. `3 + 2 × 0 = 3`, so `(3, 0)` gives 3 lots of `(1, 2)`, which is `(3, 6)`.

pages.name: A target it misses
pages.text: A target off the column space has no answer. `b = (3, 6)` is on it, and a whole line of inputs lands there. Now try `b = (3, 7)`. The rows say `x + 2y = 3` and `2x + 4y = 7`. Taking 2 lots of the first row from the second leaves `0 = 1`. That is the elimination dead end you know. Here is its cause. The second row always gives 2 lots of the first, but 7 is not 2 lots of 3.

pages.name: How many answers?
pages.task: With `A = [1 2; 2 4]`, how many answers does `Ax = (2, 5)` have?
pages.why: The rows say `x + 2y = 2` and `2x + 4y = 5`. Take 2 lots of the first row from the second. That leaves `0 = 1`. So `(2, 5)` is off the column space, and no input lands on it.

pages.name: Change one number
pages.text: The [[rank]] of a matrix is its number of independent columns. Here the columns line up, so the rank is 1. Now change the 4 to a 5. The columns of `[1 2; 2 5]` no longer line up, so its rank is 2. Only the zero arrow is crushed. The outputs fill the whole plane, and each target has exactly one answer. `b = (3, 7)` now comes from `(1, 1)` alone.

pages.name: Must it hold the origin?
pages.task: The plane `z = 1` misses the origin. Could it be a matrix’s column space?
pages.answer: No, it must hold the origin
pages.why: Zero lots of every column give the zero arrow. So every column space holds the origin. The plane `z = 1` misses it, so it is no matrix’s column space.

pages.name: The same in space
pages.text: The same holds in space. Take `A = [1 1 1; 1 2 3; 2 3 4]`. Its third row is the sum of the first two. So every output lies on the plane `z = x + y`. The columns `(1, 1, 2)` and `(1, 2, 3)` do not line up. So the rank is 2, and they reach the whole plane. The null space is the line through `(1, −2, 1)`. The input `(1, 2, 3)` lands on `(6, 14, 20)`.

pages.name: Read it as columns
pages.task: `A(1, −2, 1) = (0, 0, 0)`. Which says the same thing about A’s columns?
pages.answer: 1 lot of column 1, −2 of column 2 and 1 of column 3 add to zero
pages.why: x’s numbers say how much of each column. So `A(1, −2, 1)` is 1 lot of column 1, −2 of column 2 and 1 of column 3. `(1, 1, 2) − 2(1, 2, 3) + (1, 3, 4) = (0, 0, 0)`.

pages.name: On the plane or off it
pages.text: The rank plus the number of crushed directions is the number of columns. Each column either adds a new direction or is a mix that gives one crushed direction. Here that is `2 + 1 = 3`. The target `(6, 14, 20)` is on the plane, as `6 + 14 = 20`. Every input on `(1, 2, 3) + t(1, −2, 1)` lands on it. The target `(6, 14, 21)` is off the plane, and elimination on it ends in `0 = 1`.

pages.task: A matrix has 4 columns and rank 2. What does it crush to zero?
pages.why: The rank plus the crushed directions is the number of columns. 2 columns add new directions. The other 2 are mixes of those, and each gives one crushed direction. `4 − 2 = 2` crushed directions make a plane of inputs.
